newsitem.title: GERMANY: Mark may soon start revival from doldrums.
newsitem.headline: Mark may soon start revival from doldrums.

text.p: The mark, seeking to catch its breath against the dollar, should recover in mid-1997 and then modestly strengthen ahead of the planned 1999 start of European currency union, a Reuter survey showed on Wednesday.

The survey results showed a wide disparity of opinion on the future course of the dollar, often reflecting a range of 30 to 35 pfennigs between the highest and lowest forecasts for the seven quarters until the euro start date on January 1, 1999.

The results showed the dollar would trade at a median forecast of 1.73 marks at the end of the 1997 second quarter -- higher than the 1.59 marks posted in the survey in January that also predicted the mark would bottom in the three-month period.

Worries about the German economy should soon give way as growth expands in a low-inflation environment but doubts about a timely start to European currency union may prompt the mark to remain relatively weak against the dollar, analysts said.
"The euro factor will likely be far more important to the market than economic factors in the coming quarters," said Adolf Rosenstock at IBJ Deutschland in Frankfurt.

But others in the survey of 25 European financial institutions said Germany's economic recovery and prospects for a downturn in the U.S. would underpin the mark and could send the dollar as low as 1.50 marks in the second half of 1998.

The mark also appeared set to recover against sterling following a peak at 2.7650 marks in the second quarter before falling to 2.60 marks in the 1998 fourth quarter, according to the median forecasts in the survey.

The yen should also give back some gains against the dollar in the coming quarters after peaking at 72.46 to the mark in the second quarter and falling to 70.50 per mark in the 1998 second quarter and then to 68 per mark in the fourth quarter.

Despite the general downward dollar movement predicted by the results, some said the dollar was still not finished with its gains and would keep rising in the coming quarters, including as high as 1.90 marks in the 1998 first quarter.
In addition to a timely start for the euro, IBJ's Rosenstock said a factor favouring a higher dollar was expectations for higher short-term U.S. interest rates in the near future.

"But it goes beyond the interest rate differentials," Rosenstock said. "I expect at the end of 1997 and in early 1998 that there will be massive confusion about the risk of the euro and that will weigh on the mark."
A general view remained in Europe that a weaker mark would help spur Germany's export-led economy, which would spill over into countries who link their currency to Germany, others said.

But Germany's Commerzbank, among a group of banks including DG Bank and MM Warburg who expect the mark to recover, said the German economy was indeed set for a recovery and that currency union would likely start with a small core group excluding high-risk candidates such as Italy and Spain.

"We assume the German economy in the second half of the year will start to expand. At the moment the weaker mark helps exports and that should help for the near-term," said Matthias Hansmann, head of bond research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.
Hansmann said he expected Germany to show 1998 economic growth of about 2.8 percent, reflecting an upward trend at a time when the U.S. economy may exhibit some weakness.
"That has implications for bond markets and interest rate differential should narrow and help the mark gain against the dollar," Hansmann said.
